verdicts.strongest_argument: Both legs of this syllogism are primary-source public, and were public before the selloff the finding is built on. I rendered the instrument the hunter could not: Proclamation 11048 (FR 2026-07-23) states verbatim 'The duties imposed in this proclamation shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962', and CBP's own CSMS guidance implements it as HTS 9903.03.15 at a 0% additional rate covering 'Articles of aluminum, of steel or of copper or derivative aluminum or steel articles' - which is precisely the bucket BRP's snowmobiles and majority of ORV models were dropped into by the 6 April 2026 Section 232 derivative amendment. So the legal conclusion is right, and it is not a discovery: at least ten trade-law alerts (White & Case, Holland & Knight, Davis Wright Tremaine, Baker McKenzie, Troutman, Aprio, C.H. Robinson, GHY, Zonos, Morrison Foerster) said 'goods already subject to Section 232 are excluded' between 21 July and 24 August, several of them noting Proclamation 11048 therefore does not reach vehicles at all. Leg two - that snowmobiles and most ORVs carry 25% Section 232 on full value - is BRP's own 14 April press release and was in every wire story and the Globe and Mail. What is nowhere published is the two-step conclusion applied to DOO by name, and the tape ran the other way: DOO closed C$93.82 on 21 Aug and C$83.67 on 26 Aug, and only C$85.90 by 2 Sep, so roughly 8% of the de-rating still stands. That combination - fully published inputs, no published DOO application, contradicting price action - is the one configuration where publication is not dispositive, which is why this is 65 and not 90. Two further discounts: the causal attribution is the hunter's own, and the one piece that looked for a cause found none ('no company announcement, filing or analyst note dated August 25, 2026 was identified that would explain the move'); the 18 Aug +7.74% the finding would want as confirmation is at least as well explained by TD Securities' upgrade to Buy that same day. And Section 338 took effect 22 August - outside the quarter ended 31 July - so it can only reach this print through commentary, not through the reported numbers, competing for airtime with Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliation effective 8 September and softening North American retail.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Proclamation 11048 itself: 'The duties imposed in this proclamation shall not apply to articles subject to duties pursuant to section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962', effective 12:01 a.m. 19 August 2026.

CBP CSMS #69606660 implements the carve-out as HTS 9903.03.15 at 0% additional duty for articles of aluminum, steel or copper 'or derivative aluminum or steel articles', plus vehicles, wood, semiconductors and pharma.
Goods subject to Section 232 tariffs are exempted from the Section 338 tariffs; Proclamation 11048 therefore does not reach vehicles or auto parts and instead hits an unrelated retaliation list.

BRP's own disclosure that the 6 April 2026 Section 232 amendment applies 25% to the total value of imported snowmobiles and the majority of ORV models, replacing 50% on metal content only, at a cost in excess of $500 million.
Goods already dutiable under a Section 232 action are excluded under U.S. Note 51(c) and (d) of the Section 338 proclamations.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: Verified daily closes (stockanalysis.com, DOO/TSX): 17 Aug 88.46, 18 Aug 95.31 (+7.74%, same day as TD upgrade to Buy), 21 Aug 93.82, 24 Aug 88.25 (-5.94%), 25 Aug 85.09, 26 Aug 83.67, then 86.10 / 86.05 / 85.57 / 85.83 / 85.90 into 2 Sep. So ~2.7 of the ~10.8 points have come back and ~8% stands unreversed - which is the finding's best evidence that it is not priced, and simultaneously evidence that the market saw the published carve-out and did not act on it. Baseline spot 63.67 (USD, ~C$85.9 at 1.349) and run_up_20d -1.23% are consistent with this series. Options carry no statement: ATM spread 65% of mid, put/call OI 0.01, skew null. Reaction history in the baseline discarded as instructed; from BRP's real release dates I can only recover 2025-12-04 +6.39%, 2026-03-26 +3.45%, 2026-05-28 +0.93% - three prints, all up, none large, and 2026-01-29 and 2026-04-22 in that list are not earnings.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A BRP 6-K, IR statement or sell-side note between 22 August and today that names Section 338 and BRP's exemption would push this to 90; conversely, evidence that any BRP Canada-origin US-bound SKU (Can-Am Spyder/Ryker from Valcourt, Canada-finished PA&A) sits in the Annex II list outside the 9903.03.15 zero-rate bucket would cut the size and drop this below 50.

verdicts.strongest_argument: The negative claim is correct and I verified it independently: BRP's Q1 FY27 press release (6-K exhibit 99.1, 28 May 2026) contains no mention of IEEPA, tariff refund, duty refund or tariff recovery; the FY26 MD&A (40-F exhibit 99.3) mentions IEEPA nowhere and quantifies no tariff cost at all, saying only 'the unfavourable impacts of global tariffs mainly on PA&A'; and the Q1 FY27 call did not discuss IEEPA or refunds. So the finding's fact pattern holds. What keeps this off a low score is that every ingredient is a headline, not an obscurity: the Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs 6-3 on 20 February 2026, a court ordered the government to begin refunding ~$130bn, the CBP refund portal opened 20 April 2026, and the direct comparable - the only other name the same analysts cover - published its exact number in its 28 July release, where the $74m refund was $0.96 of a $1.97 adjusted EPS and led the coverage. Any desk modelling DOO's July quarter has had 'does BRP get a Polaris-style refund' in front of it for five weeks; that question is canvassed even if the answer is not in consensus. Three things cut the size hard. First, the mechanism is much narrower for BRP than for Polaris: BRP's entire tariff problem as it has described it is Section 232, because USMCA-originating goods were carved out of the IEEPA Canada and Mexico orders from 7 March 2025, so BRP's finished vehicles from Valcourt, Juarez and Queretaro plausibly paid no IEEPA duty at all - only the directly-US-entered Asia-sourced PA&A did, and the China portion of that carries Section 301 duties which are not refundable. Second, BRP has never sized its tariff drag, so 'mainly on PA&A' is not a number; against FY26 revenue and a gross-profit line where a $28.5m EV provision was 116bps, a refundable IEEPA slice of C$20-50m is the realistic band, i.e. C$0.25-0.65 of one-time EPS on a C$85.90 share. Third, and least obvious, BRP reports under IFRS: IAS 37 permits recognition of a contingent asset only when realisation is virtually certain, a stricter gate than the US GAAP judgement Polaris made, and the refund process has been widely described as messy and appealable - so BRP can be fully entitled and still disclose rather than book, which would make this a non-event tomorrow.

prior_publication.what_it_says: The Supreme Court ended the IEEPA tariffs, invalidating both the reciprocal and drug-trafficking tariffs and opening a refund question for importers.

Polaris recorded a $74m benefit in the quarter for IEEPA tariff refund claims, contributing $0.96 to adjusted EPS of $1.97 - the read-across the finding relies on, published five weeks ago in a widely-read transcript.
The CBP IEEPA refund portal opened 20 April 2026; the government owes importers an estimated $166bn plus interest.
USMCA-qualifying goods were exempted from the IEEPA Canada and Mexico tariffs from 7 March 2025 - the reason BRP's Canada- and Mexico-built vehicles likely paid no refundable IEEPA duty.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: No move I can attribute to a BRP refund. The stock's August path is entirely a Section 338 / trade-escalation path (95.31 on 18 Aug to 83.67 on 26 Aug, 85.90 on 2 Sep); 28 July, the day Polaris disclosed its $74m, produced no visible DOO re-rating in the run-up series (20d run-up -1.23%). Options give no read - put/call OI 0.01, ATM spread 65% of mid, skew null - so I cannot say downside or upside is bid. Consensus for Q2 FY27 anchors on BRP's own 28 May guidance of EPS down ~$1.60-1.65 y/y, which contains no refund, so a refund would be a genuine beat against the published number rather than something already in estimates.
verdicts.what_would_change_it: Any evidence of the dollar size of BRP's directly-US-entered IEEPA-dutiable imports - a quantified FY26 tariff figure, a customs-data estimate, or a sell-side note carrying a BRP refund line - would move this either way; a BRP statement that its US imports were USMCA-originating and paid no IEEPA duty would take it to 95 by killing the mechanism.

verdicts.strongest_argument: This restates published guidance and a company press release. On the Q1 FY27 call on 28 May 2026 management told the market in terms not to expect price to carry the tariff: 'don't expect any brutal move on pricing', with increases 'less' than low single-digit percentages, to protect competitive positioning - three months before the MY27 price sheet the finding treats as the reveal. The margin arithmetic is also already given: CAD 500-550m gross incremental tariff impact for FY27 (CAD 650-700m annualised), CAD 200m of mitigation, net CAD 3.10-3.60 per share, and revised FY27 guidance of $9.1-9.4bn revenue and $3.00-3.50 normalised EPS. 'Absorbing the tariff in margin rather than pricing it' is not an inference from the price sheet; it is the guidance. The price sheet itself is then BRP's own newswire release of 17 August ('Can-Am Unveils 2027 Side-by-Side and All-Terrain Vehicles', PR Newswire) plus trade coverage that already draws the conclusion - RideApart and SXS Nation describe BRP adding factory-installed content and selectively lowering prices on Commander, Defender and Outlander specifically 'to drive sales and offset the impact of tariffs'. One sub-claim is simply wrong: the CAD 200m plan is not only overhead and lean - the Q1 call lists 'targeted pricing adjustments' and value-chain efficiencies among its components alongside overhead discipline and a CAD 350m/three-year lean programme. Reach is also weak: MY27 ORV shipments begin around August, so this price sheet lands in Q3 FY27 onward and touches the quarter ended 31 July only through outlook commentary, and the Q2 EPS decline of ~$1.60-1.65 was pre-announced on 28 May. The residual 12 is for the possibility that the specific magnitude - near-1% list pricing plus outright cuts plus added free content, against a 25% ad valorem cost - is a worse net price/mix than a consensus that read 'targeted pricing adjustments' more generously.

prior_publication.what_it_says: Management guides CAD 500-550m gross tariff impact, CAD 200m mitigation including 'targeted pricing adjustments', net CAD 3.10-3.60 per share, and says 'don't expect any brutal move on pricing' with increases below low single digits.
BRP's own newswire release unveiling the MY27 Can-Am off-road line with the pricing and added factory-installed content the finding describes.
Revised FY27 guidance of $9.1-9.4bn revenue and $3.00-3.50 normalised EPS 'incorporating incremental tariff cost net of mitigation measures', i.e. the margin absorption is in the published number.
Trade coverage stating BRP is adding factory-installed equipment and selectively lowering MY27 off-road prices to drive sales and offset tariffs - the finding's interpretation, already in print.

verdicts.baseline_evidence: The MY27 reveal week produced no de-rating: 17 Aug closed 88.46 and 18 Aug closed 95.31 (+7.74%), and the stock was still 93.82 on 21 Aug - four sessions after the price sheet was public. Whatever the market did with this information, it was not sell it. The subsequent 24-26 Aug decline maps to Section 338 taking effect and Canada suspending negotiations, not to a price list published a week earlier. No options read available (put/call OI 0.01, skew null).
verdicts.what_would_change_it: A dealer-level or per-unit net-price computation showing MY27 realised price/mix materially below the 'targeted pricing adjustments' embedded in the CAD 200m plan, or evidence that consensus gross margin for H2 FY27 assumes pricing BRP has now foregone, would pull this down toward 55.

interactions: Findings #0 and #2 rest on the same document: BRP's 14 April 2026 release and the 28 May Q1 FY27 call, which together establish the 25%-of-full-value Section 232 derivative treatment of snowmobiles and most ORVs. #0 uses that fact to argue the incremental Section 338 exposure is nil; #2 uses the same fact to argue margin is being surrendered. They are not contradictory - the 232 cost is undisputed and only the 338 increment is at issue - but they cannot both be scored as novel from one shared disclosure, and #0's whole legal argument depends on #2's premise being exactly as BRP stated it. #2 additionally contains a factual error against its own shared source: the Q1 call lists 'targeted pricing adjustments' as a component of the CAD 200m mitigation plan, contradicting the finding's assertion that the plan is 'overhead and lean initiatives, not price'. #0 and #1 are both directionally positive and both would be resolved by the same MD&A and the same call tomorrow, so they are not independent bets - if management declines to quantify (its consistent practice: no tariff dollar figure appears in the FY26 MD&A or the Q1 FY27 release), both stall together.
